title: How do you optimize Kafka for high throughput (batch.size, linger.ms, compression, acks, max.in.flight)?
shortTitle: How do you optimize Kafka for high throughput (batch.size, linger.ms, compression, acks, max.in.flight)?
keyPoints: batch.size controls how many bytes accumulate per partition before sending; larger batches mean fewer, more efficient requests.
linger.ms tells the producer to wait a few milliseconds so batches fill up; essential because a large batch.size does nothing if batches ship half-empty.
compression.type (lz4, zstd) shrinks the batch, and larger batches compress better, so linger and compression reinforce each other.
acks=all should be kept for banking correctness; squeeze throughput from batching and compression instead of weakening durability.
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection (up to 5) lets several batches travel at once; with idempotence, ordering is still guaranteed.
buffer.memory must be raised if the producer accumulates many batches, otherwise send() blocks or throws.
More partitions allow more parallelism on both producer and consumer sides.

s1_definition.oneliner: Bigger batches plus a little linger plus compression plus several in-flight requests maximize throughput, while acks and in-flight settings keep you safe from loss and reordering.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **batch.size** -- how many bytes accumulate per partition before sending; default 16 KB, increase for throughput.
- **linger.ms** -- how long to wait to fill a batch; default 0 (send immediately), increase to 5-20 ms for better batching.
- **compression.type** -- shrinks the batch end to end (none, gzip, snappy, lz4, zstd); lz4 and zstd are fast and effective.
- **acks** -- durability level; keep `all` for banking and optimize throughput elsewhere.
- **max.in.flight.requests.per.connection** -- how many unacknowledged batches fly at once; up to 5 with idempotence preserves ordering.
- **buffer.memory** -- total bytes the producer can use for batching; raise if many partitions or large batches.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sending transaction forms to the central office. Instead of one courier trip per form, the clerk waits a few seconds to collect a stack. A bigger envelope means fewer trips. Compressing the stack makes the envelope lighter. Several couriers on the road at once means more mail per minute. But waiting too long delays each form, so there is a balance.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Throughput Optimization

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Producer                                     │
  │                                               │
  │ Records ──▶ Batch buffer (batch.size=64KB)   │
  │              │                                │
  │              │ linger.ms=10 (wait to fill)    │
  │              ▼                                │
  │           Full batch                          │
  │              │                                │
  │              │ compression=lz4 (shrink)       │
  │              ▼                                │
  │           Compressed batch                    │
  │              │                                │
  │              │ max.in.flight=5                 │
  │              │ (5 batches flying at once)     │
  │              ▼                                │
  │         ─── Network ───▶ Broker               │
  │              ▲                                │
  │              │ acks=all (safe)                │
  │              │ ack arrives                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To optimize Kafka for high throughput, tune five knobs together. Increase batch.size so more records accumulate per request. Add linger.ms of 5-20 milliseconds so batches actually fill up. Enable compression (lz4 or zstd) to shrink batches, which saves network and disk end to end. Keep acks=all for banking correctness and get throughput from batching instead. Set max.in.flight to 5 with idempotence so multiple batches fly at once without risking reordering.

The knobs interact: a big batch.size does nothing without linger.ms because batches ship half-empty. Compression amplifies larger batches because more repetitive data compresses better. Raise buffer.memory if accumulating many batches.

At National Bank of India, the end-of-day job published millions of transaction events. The naive one-record-at-a-time producer could not keep up, but after setting 64 KB batches, 10 ms linger, lz4 compression, and 5 in-flight requests with idempotence, throughput jumped by an order of magnitude while durability stayed at acks=all.

Remember one sentence: bigger batches plus a little linger plus compression plus multiple in-flight requests maximize throughput, and you never weaken acks in banking.
